JPMorgan Chase adopted ASU 2022-02, *Financial Instruments – Credit Losses: Troubled Debt Restructurings ("TDRs")*, on **January 1, 2023**, under the **modified retrospective method**. The 2023 Form 10-K (Note 1, "Accounting standards adopted January 1, 2023"; Note 13; MD&A "Allowance for Credit Losses") discloses the following amounts, all in millions of dollars:

### 1. Allowance for credit losses: **net decrease of $587 million** (pretax)

This is the "Cumulative effect of a change in accounting principle" line in the allowance for loan losses rollforward (Note 13 and MD&A, both p. 258 / p. 132 of the 10-K):

| Portfolio segment | Amount ($M) |
|---|---|
| Consumer, excluding credit card | **(489)** |
| Credit card | **(100)** |
| Wholesale | **+2** |
| **Total (allowance for loan losses)** | **(587)** |
| Allowance for lending-related commitments | NA (no impact) |
| Allowance for credit losses on investment securities | NA (no impact) |

**What it measures:** The pretax reduction in management's estimate of expected credit losses over the remaining expected life of retained loans. It arises because the new guidance eliminated TDR accounting and disclosure (including the requirement to measure TDR-related allowances using a discounted cash flow methodology and the pre-modification effective interest rate as the discount rate). JPMorgan elected its non-DCF, portfolio-based allowance approach for loans modified for borrowers experiencing financial difficulty ("FDMs") for all portfolios except collateral-dependent loans and nonaccrual risk-rated loans, for which the asset-specific (DCF) approach continues. The 10-K states the impact was "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card." Note also that no business-segment (CCB/CIB/CB/AWM) breakout of the adoption effect is disclosed; the only breakdown given is by loan portfolio segment.

### 2. Retained earnings: **increase of $446 million** (after-tax)

**What it measures:** The after-tax cumulative-effect adjustment to opening (January 1, 2023) retained earnings recorded in the Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity from the adoption — i.e., the $587 million pretax allowance release net of the related income tax benefit (implying roughly $141 million of tax benefit). It reflects that the reduced expected credit losses on previously modified (troubled) loans flow through retained earnings rather than through 2023 provision expense, and is likewise "predominantly driven by residential real estate and credit card."

### 3. Related equity-statement presentation

The Consolidated statements of changes in stockholders' equity show a 2023 line "Cumulative effect of change in accounting principles" of **$449 million** added to retained earnings. This is the combined effect of the TDR guidance ($446 million) and the concurrently adopted *Derivatives and Hedging: Fair Value Hedging – Portfolio Layer Method* guidance, whose impact on retained earnings (from transferring HTM securities to AFS and designating them in portfolio-layer hedges) the 10-K states "was not material."

### Related 2023 disclosure changes (context, not adoption effects)

The same guidance eliminated TDR disclosures and the "reasonably expected"/"concession" tests, replaced them with FDM disclosure (principal forgiveness, interest rate reduction, other-than-insignificant payment delay, term extension), and added gross charge-offs by vintage origination year. Under the new criteria, 2023 FDMs were $136 million for residential real estate and $648 million for credit card.

> "We expect to incur costs of approximately $700 million in connection with separating Upjohn, of which, approximately 75% has been incurred since inception and through December 31, 2021. These charges include costs and expenses related to separation of legal entities and transaction costs."

This is the total, forward-looking figure, and it names the two cost categories you asked about: (a) costs and expenses related to **separation of legal entities**, and (b) **transaction costs**. The filing also quantifies the portion already spent: approximately 75% incurred since inception through December 31, 2021 (i.e., roughly $525 million of the $700 million).

**2. Actual separation-related costs incurred — "$434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019"**

From Note 2B, "Divestitures — Upjohn Separation and Combination with Mylan" (10-K p. 65):

> "As a result of the separation of Upjohn, we incurred separation-related costs of $434 million in 2020 and $83 million in 2019, which are included in *Discontinued operations—net of tax*. These costs primarily relate to professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities within finance, tax, legal and information system functions as well as investment banking fees."

So the incurred amounts are $434 million (2020) and $83 million (2019) — $517 million cumulative, consistent with the ~75% of $700 million figure. Note the composition stated here is narrower in wording than the MD&A: it covers **professional fees for regulatory filings**, separation activities in the **finance, tax, legal and information system** functions, and **investment banking fees** (i.e., the transaction-cost element). These amounts are reported within *Discontinued operations—net of tax* on the consolidated statements of income, and the non-GAAP reconciliation confirms that "Discontinued operations" adjustments relate primarily to the spin-off of the Upjohn Business and the sale of Meridian.

NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 Form 10-K (FY ended January 25, 2026) gives several related reasons across MD&A, Item 7A, and the notes to the financial statements:

**1. No readily determinable fair value / no market prices (Note 1, accounting policy)**
NVIDIA states that non-marketable equity securities "consist of investments in privately-held companies that do not have a readily determinable fair value." They are carried at cost minus impairment and adjusted for observable price changes in orderly transactions for an identical or similar investment in the same issuer (the "measurement alternative"). Critically, the filing says: "Fair value is based upon observable inputs in an inactive market and the valuation requires our judgment due to the absence of market prices and inherent lack of liquidity."

**2. Lack of readily available market data and observable transactions, plus macroeconomic factors (Item 7A, page 45)**
"Valuations of our non-marketable equity securities are inherently complex due to the lack of readily available market data and observable transactions, and impact of macroeconomic factors."

**3. Need for unobservable inputs (Critical Accounting Estimates, page 38; Note 8, pages 66–67)**
Under the measurement alternative, "These adjustments may require use of unobservable inputs." Note 8 specifies the valuation methods rely on observable transactions for similar investments of the same issuer plus unobservable inputs such as volatility, expected time to liquidity, risk-free rate, and security-specific rights and obligations. Because these are unobservable, the amounts are inherently uncertain and sensitive to assumptions.

**4. Impairment assessment requires judgment (Critical Accounting Estimates)**
NVIDIA "assesses impairment quarterly based on qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee's operating performance and market trends," writing investments down to fair value if impairment is identified — a forward-looking determination rather than a market-quoted price.

**5. Illiquidity and the early-stage nature of the investees (Risk Factors, page 22)**

Berkshire's 2024 Form 10-K gives the explanation in two places, which together state the reasons.

**1. Management's Discussion and Analysis (page K-43, BHE section).** Immediately after presenting BHE's summary of net earnings (revenues, costs, pre-tax earnings, income tax benefit, and net earnings after income taxes for 2024–2022), the filing states:

> "The discussion of BHE's operating results that follows is based on after-tax earnings, reflecting how the energy businesses are managed and evaluated."

**2. Note 26, "Business segment data" (page K-109).** Here the filing draws the explicit contrast the question asks about:

> "For most non-insurance businesses, pre-tax earnings are considered in allocating resources and capital, **although income taxes are also considered at BHE, given the magnitude of production tax credits associated with wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation.**"

### Why this matters for BHE specifically

The tax effects at BHE are unusually large and work in the opposite direction from a normal corporate tax burden:

- BHE's summary of net earnings shows an **income tax benefit** of $1,871 million (2024), $2,022 million (2023) and $1,629 million (2022), with the footnote that the benefit "*Includes significant production tax credits primarily from wind-powered electricity generation.*" The resulting **effective income tax rates are negative** — (81.6)% in 2024, (215.1)% in 2023 and (51.8)% in 2022.
- Because of this, pre-tax earnings materially understate BHE's economics: 2024 pre-tax earnings of $2,292 million became $4,163 million of net earnings after income taxes. A pre-tax presentation would strip out the wind production tax credits and the associated regulatory mechanics that are central to how the energy businesses actually earn money.
- The filing also notes (page K-43) that "The rates BHE's regulated businesses charge customers for energy and services are largely based on the costs of business operations, **including income taxes** and a return on capital, and are subject to regulatory approval." Taxes are thus embedded in BHE's regulated revenue model, and the resulting tax credits/benefits flow back into results through the regulatory rate-setting process — another reason an after-tax view is the economically meaningful measure for this segment.

In short: the filing's stated reason is that (a) BHE is managed and evaluated on an after-tax basis, and (b) unlike other non-insurance businesses, income taxes are a material consideration in allocating resources and capital at BHE because of the magnitude of production tax credits from wind-powered electricity generation investments and the related impacts from regulation.

ExxonMobil's 2023 Form 10-K attributes the drop in Upstream realizations to two headline causes, as stated in the **2023 Upstream Earnings Factor Analysis** (p. 53):

> "**Price** – Lower realizations decreased earnings by **$14,290 million** reflecting **lower gas prices** and **crude price moderation with growing liquids supply to address record demand**, and unfavorable mark-to-market impacts of **$2,380 million**."

That price factor, together with volume/mix (+$970M), other (−$100M) and identified items (−$2,301M, mainly the Santa Ynez impairment), drove Upstream earnings from $36.479B in 2022 to $21.308B in 2023 (p. 53).

## The underlying market causes ("Recent Business Environment," p. 51)

The filing explains the price declines as a normalization from the exceptional 2022 conditions:

**Background — why 2022 was high**
- Pre-COVID underinvestment in capacity, accelerated by the pandemic collapse in industry revenue, produced underinvestment and supply tightness as demand recovered.
- Industry rationalization took more than 3 million b/d of refining capacity offline, compounded by supply chain constraints — driving a steady increase in oil, gas prices and refining margins through 2022.

**2023 causes — crude oil**
- "During the first half of 2023, the price of crude oil declined towards the average of the pre-COVID 10-year range (2010-2019), **impacted by higher inventory levels**."
- "In the second half, crude oil prices increased modestly from **strong demand** and **ongoing actions by OPEC+ oil producers to limit supply**."
- In the earnings factor analysis this is summarized as **"growing liquids supply to address record demand"** — i.e., new supply coming online to meet record demand (plus inventory build) caused price moderation.

**2023 causes — natural gas**
- "In the first nine months of the year, natural gas prices declined significantly with **storage levels increasing above historical averages in the United States and Europe on higher supply and lower demand**."
- "In the fourth quarter, natural gas prices improved as **higher heating demand in the U.S.** and **supply interruptions in Europe and Asia** brought prices back above the 10-year range."

**Macro overlay**
- Inflation "moderated in 2023 as major central banks **tightened monetary policy aggressively** and **global GDP growth slowed**" — weighing on demand, particularly gas.

## Causes of the $2.6 billion increase in consumer net charge-offs in 2023

**1. Card Services (credit card) — the predominant driver (~$2.3 billion of the increase)**

The 10-K attributes the increase "predominantly driven by Card Services, as the portfolio continued to normalize to pre-pandemic levels" (Consolidated Results of Operations, p. 56; CCB results, p. 69). Supporting detail:
- Credit card loans grew "from growth from new accounts and revolving balances which continued to normalize to pre-pandemic levels" (p. 119), enlarging the balance on which losses were incurred.
- "Net charge-offs increased for the year ended December 31, 2023 compared to the prior year as delinquencies have normalized" (p. 119). The 30+ day delinquency rate rose to 2.14% from 1.45%, and the 90+ day rate to 1.05% from 0.68%.
- Gross card charge-offs rose to $5,491 million from $3,192 million (Note 12, p. 246); Card Services net charge-offs were $4,699 million vs. $2,403 million, a 2.45% net charge-off rate vs. 1.47% (p. 72).

**2. Scored auto loans — decline in used vehicle valuations (~$189 million of the increase)**

"Net charge-offs for the year ended December 31, 2023 increased compared to the prior year due to higher charge-offs of scored auto loans driven by the decline in used vehicle valuations" (p. 118). The scored auto net charge-off rate rose to 0.56% from 0.24%; Auto segment net charge-offs were $357 million vs. $144 million, a 0.49% rate vs. 0.21% (p. 72).

**3. Residential real estate — lower recoveries (~$174 million of the increase)**

Because net charge-offs are net of recoveries, the residential real estate book contributed to the increase even with lower gross charge-offs: "Net recoveries were lower for the year ended December 31, 2023 compared to the prior year driven by lower prepayments due to higher interest rates" (p. 119). Residential real estate recorded net recoveries of $52 million in 2023 versus $226 million in 2022 (p. 117), i.e., recoveries offset a smaller amount of gross charge-offs.

**Note on measurement:** the $2.6 billion is the firmwide consumer increase ($5,330 million of net charge-offs in 2023 vs. $2,672 million in 2022, p. 117), which the 10-K reconciles as "$2.6 billion in consumer, predominantly driven by Card Services, as the portfolio continued to normalize to pre-pandemic levels" (p. 56). It excludes the separate $1.9 billion net addition to the consumer allowance for credit losses (a provision, not a charge-off), which was driven mainly by Card Services loan growth and, in Home Lending, was a net reduction.

## The change and Pfizer's stated cause

Net cash provided by operating activities rose from $8,700 million in 2023 to $12,744 million in 2024, an increase of $4,044 million (Pfizer describes it as a 46% increase in its Financial Highlights).

Pfizer's own explanation, in the "Drivers of change 2024 v. 2023" column, is that the change **"was driven primarily by an increase in net income adjusted for non-cash items partially offset by the timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business, including a decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid and net changes in inventory greater than one year (see Note 8A)."**

## The positive driver

The "increase in net income adjusted for non-cash items" is visible in the cash flow statement. Net income from continuing operations before allocation to noncontrolling interests rose from $2,172 million to $8,051 million, and the non-cash add-backs were also higher or more favorable:

- Depreciation and amortization rose from $6,290 million to $7,013 million (higher Seagen-related intangible amortization and asset base).
- Asset write-offs and impairments rose from $3,408 million to $4,242 million.
- Share-based compensation expense rose from $525 million to $877 million.
- The $6,199 million of "Inventory write-offs and related charges associated with COVID-19 products" recorded in 2023 (Paxlovid $5.0 billion and Comirnaty $1.2 billion) did not recur in 2024 — a major contributor to the 46% increase in pretax continuing income to $8.0 billion, with the related $7.1 billion decrease in cost of sales (also helped by a $2.6 billion favorable sales mix, and offset by a $1.9 billion Seagen impact including amortization of the fair value step-up of inventory).
- 2023 was also depressed by the $3.5 billion **non-cash** Paxlovid revenue reversal recorded in the fourth quarter of 2023, which did not recur in 2024 (though 2024 included a $771 million favorable final adjustment to that reversal and $442 million from the one-time contractual delivery of Paxlovid courses to the U.S. Strategic National Stockpile).

## Offsetting factors

**1. Timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business.** Pfizer identifies this as the principal offset, and within it specifically:

- **A decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid.** Note 17C shows deferred revenues related to Paxlovid and Comirnaty falling from $5.1 billion at December 31, 2023 to $2.2 billion at December 31, 2024 ($2.6 billion/$2.5 billion current/noncurrent in 2023 versus $1.4 billion/$785 million in 2024). The decline was driven by amounts recognized in product revenues as products were delivered (including the $442 million U.S. SNS delivery) and the $771 million favorable Paxlovid adjustment, partially offset by additional advance payments received in 2024 under amended contracts. Pfizer recognized approximately $2.9 billion of the prior-year deferred revenue balance during 2024. Because the cash was received in prior years, the 2024 recognition of that revenue is a non-cash boost to net income and a working-capital drag on operating cash flow.
- Other working-capital drags visible in the statement were larger in 2024 than 2023: trade accounts payable (a $1,023 million use of cash vs. a $300 million use in 2023); other liabilities (a $3,115 million use vs. a $595 million source); other tax accounts, net (a $1,345 million use vs. a $982 million use); trade accounts receivable (a $109 million use vs. a $347 million source); and a smaller deferred-tax add-back ($2,102 million vs. $3,442 million). A favorable swing of $4,043 million did occur in "Other assets" (a $3,380 million source of cash in 2024 vs. a $663 million use in 2023), which is the balance sheet line that carries the noncurrent inventory balances.

**2. Net changes in inventory greater than one year** (inventories not expected to be sold within 12 months) — Pfizer lists this as the other offsetting factor and cross-references Note 8A for the cause.

## The cause Pfizer gives for the change in inventories not expected to be sold within one year

Under its accounting policy (Note 1I), inventories that are not expected to be sold within 12 months are classified within **Other noncurrent assets** on the balance sheet. Note 8A reports:

- Noncurrent inventories: **$2,663 million at December 31, 2024 vs. $4,568 million at December 31, 2023** (a decrease of $1,905 million).
- Pfizer's stated cause: *"The decrease from December 31, 2023 is primarily driven by a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, inclusive of the acquisition accounting fair value step-up."* It cross-references Note 2A.
- Pfizer adds: *"Based on our current estimates and assumptions, there are no recoverability issues for these amounts."*

Supporting context: at the December 14, 2023 Seagen acquisition Pfizer recognized $3,273 million of inventories on a fair-value basis (comprising $1.1 billion current and $2.1 billion noncurrent), so the 2024 noncurrent balance decline largely reflects the sell-through of that acquired, fair-value-stepped-up Seagen inventory. The corresponding income-statement effect appears in cost of sales, where the $1.9 billion "impact from our Seagen acquisition, inclusive of the amortization of the fair value step-up of inventory" was an offsetting factor to the 2024 cost-of-sales decline.

By contrast, the *current* Inventories balance **increased** to $10,851 million from $10,189 million, which Note 8A attributes to "higher inventory levels for certain products mainly due to changes in net market demand, network strategy and new product launches" — the opposite direction from the noncurrent balance.

It is also worth noting that the year-over-year comparison is not like-for-like: the 2023 decline in noncurrent inventories (from $5,827 million at December 31, 2022) was driven by COVID-19 product write-offs — $4.2 billion for Paxlovid and $0.7 billion for Comirnaty — offset by approximately $3.1 billion of acquired Seagen inventory including the fair value step-up, with no recoverability issues. In 2024, by contrast, the driver is the reduction of the acquired Seagen inventory (including the fair value step-up) rather than COVID-19 write-offs, since the $6.2 billion of 2023 COVID-19 inventory charges did not recur.

## Summary

Pfizer attributes the increase in operating cash flow from $8.7 billion to $12.7 billion primarily to higher net income adjusted for non-cash items (boosted by the non-recurrence of the $6.2 billion of 2023 COVID-19 inventory write-offs, higher depreciation/amortization and impairments, and the absence of the 2023 non-cash $3.5 billion Paxlovid revenue reversal), partially offset by the timing of receipts and payments in the ordinary course of business — notably the decrease in advance payments for Comirnaty and Paxlovid (deferred revenues down from $5.1 billion to $2.2 billion) — and by net changes in inventory greater than one year. For that last item, Pfizer's cause is a reduction in acquired Seagen inventory, inclusive of the acquisition accounting fair value step-up, with no recoverability issues.

## Answer: Two of the eight filings

### 1. Pfizer Inc. — 2025 Form 10-K → **Haleon** (Haleon plc)

Note 2C, "Equity-Method Investments" (p. 75 of the filing):

> "After the October 2024 share sale, we owned approximately 15% of the outstanding voting shares of Haleon as of December 31, 2024. **We sold the remaining portion of our investment in Haleon for $6.3 billion and recognized a net loss on the sale of $144 million in the first quarter of 2025** in Other (income)/deductions––net."

Haleon was a publicly traded London Stock Exchange–listed company (the GSK/Pfizer consumer-healthcare joint venture) held purely as an investment, not a subsidiary or operating business. The March and October 2024 partial sales brought ownership to ~15%; the Q1 2025 sale was a complete exit. Note 4 corroborates the loss. (Note: Pfizer's ~11.7% interest in ViiV was **not** sold in 2025 — only dividend income of $265 million was recognized, and the 10-K describes a ViiV sale as only "planned.")

### 2. Walmart Inc. — fiscal 2025 Form 10-K → **JD.com** (JD.com, Inc.)

Note 8, "Fair Value Measurements," subsection "Sale of Investment" (p. 70):

> "**In August 2024, the Company sold its investment in JD.com for net proceeds of approximately $3.6 billion and recorded a realized loss of $0.3 billion** within other gains and losses."

MD&A (Liquidity) confirms: investing cash flow was partly offset by "net proceeds received from sales of certain strategic investments, **including $3.6 billion related to the sale of our JD.com investment**." JD.com was a minority-stake equity investment (not a consolidated subsidiary and not a retail operation), and the August 2024 date falls inside Walmart's fiscal 2025 (Feb. 1, 2024 – Jan. 31, 2025). The $4.2 billion decline in the fair value of Walmart's equity investments during fiscal 2025 is attributed "primarily due to the sale of the Company's investment in JD.com," consistent with a full exit.
